name: Meclofenoxate (Centrophenoxine)

card.summary: DMAE ester nootropic with 1970s elderly-memory studies and a mouse-lifespan claim behind its "anti-aging" reputation; no studies of skin.
card.note: Not FDA-approved; prescription-only in places such as Germany and Japan; sold as a supplement in the US.

quick.overview:
Meclofenoxate (centrophenoxine) is an ester of dimethylaminoethanol (DMAE) and 4-chlorophenoxyacetic acid. It is sold as a prescription drug in Japan and some European countries, under names such as Lucidril, and as a supplement in the US.

Its "anti-aging" reputation rests on lipofuscin (age pigment) findings in the brain and a reported 26.5 percent lifespan increase in mice. A 1977 study reported improved memory-test performance in elderly patients. No studies have tested it on skin.
quick.mechanism: It is classed as a cholinergic nootropic; animal studies report changes in brain monoamines and protection in cerebral ischemia models.
quick.risks: Rare effects include insomnia, dizziness, restlessness, tremor, depression, nausea and headache, which Wikipedia says may reflect overdose. Brazil lists it as a controlled substance (2023) and it is not FDA-approved.

lead: Meclofenoxate, also known as centrophenoxine (brand names include Lucidril), is an ester of dimethylethanolamine (DMAE) and 4-chlorophenoxyacetic acid. It is sold as a prescription drug in Japan and some European countries including Germany, Hungary and Austria, and as a dietary supplement in the United States, where it is not FDA-approved.[1][13] Its name reflects its structure: after it is absorbed, it is described as breaking down into DMAE, a choline precursor, and a chlorophenoxyacetic acid fragment.[1][17][3]

People interested in healthy-looking aging discuss it mainly through an 'anti-aging' chain: it is said to clear lipofuscin, the age-linked pigment that accumulates in cells, which supporters connect to sharper cognition and a younger functional profile. DMAE-containing compounds also appear in some topical skin-firming products, though research on meclofenoxate itself and skin appearance has not been published.[1][2]

Published human research is mostly from the 1960s to the 1980s and includes controlled trials in elderly volunteers and in patients with dementia-related syndromes, plus a larger body of animal work. A 26.5 percent lifespan increase reported in mice for meclofenoxate and DMAE and a 1977 elderly memory study are the basis of its longevity reputation.[1][6]

paras: Meclofenoxate is not a topical product. Its appearance-related reputation rests on the idea that it slows age-related change from the inside, with lipofuscin reduction as the headline mechanism that proponents cite.[3][4] No studies of meclofenoxate on skin aging have been found.

In Japan and several European countries the drug has been prescribed for cognitive decline in older adults and for post-traumatic dizziness, and it appears in the clinical literature on organic psychosyndrome and neurasthenic syndromes.[8][9][10][12] Cholinergic drugs including meclofenoxate have also been examined in systematic reviews for antipsychotic-induced tardive dyskinesia.[11]

A 1977 double-blind study by Marcer and Hopkins in Age and Ageing tested meclofenoxate on memory performance in fit, able elderly volunteers and reported that it appeared to increase consolidation of new information, with effects differing across the memory measures.[6]

A 1968 double-blind controlled trial in Folia Psychiatrica et Neurologica Japonica examined Lucidril in the post-traumatic syndrome, especially dizziness.[8] A 1983 double-blind placebo-controlled study in Der Nervenarzt covered centrophenoxine in neurasthenic syndromes.[9] Two 1989-1990 trials in Archives of Gerontology and Geriatrics studied centrophenoxine in elderly people with organic psychosyndrome, one using a gerontopsychological inventory and one measuring body composition and biochemical parameters.[10][12]

A 1978 study measured lipofuscin pigment, cytoplasmic RNA and nucleolar volume in the nerve cells of patients with senile dementia, noting earlier reports that meclofenoxate improves mental performance and reduces neuronal lipofuscin.[7] A registered trial of about 300 participants combines meclofenoxate with coenzyme Q10 in hepatic encephalopathy.[5]

Rare effects described for meclofenoxate are insomnia, dizziness, restlessness, tremor, depression, nausea, muscle tension and headache, which may relate to higher intake.[1] It is generally prescription-only where marketed as a drug, Brazil classified it as a controlled substance in 2023, and it is unapproved in the US.[1]
A 2022 toxicology paper and a 2023 review describe centrophenoxine as an unapproved or unauthorized ingredient in cognitive-enhancement dietary supplements.[13][15]

Wikipedia lists it as a cholinergic agent.[1] After administration, meclofenoxate is hydrolysed to DMAE, whose metabolism in mouse brain and liver was followed in a 1976 study.[3] Rat studies reported raised brain choline levels and compared the effects of meclofenoxate on noradrenaline, dopamine and serotonin with other nootropics.[4][16] In rats with chronic cerebral ischemia, centrophenoxine improved cognitive deficits and neuronal degeneration.[2] Grokipedia (AI-generated) additionally describes lipofuscin reduction in animal models.[17]
Meclofenoxate has the formula C12H16ClNO3 and is the ester of DMAE and 4-chlorophenoxyacetic acid.[1]

sections.h: Relationship to DMAE and skin products
paras: Dimethylethanolamine (DMAE) is a small molecule that Wikipedia describes as used in skin care products to improve skin tone, and, taken orally, as a nootropic sold in supplement form as a bitartrate salt; the same article notes animal tests suggesting possible memory benefits and reports no human efficacy data.[23] Meclofenoxate is the ester of DMAE with 4-chlorophenoxyacetic acid and is not itself a cosmetic ingredient.[1] For people interested in looks, the connection is therefore indirect: topical DMAE products are marketed for firmer-looking skin, while meclofenoxate is discussed as an oral compound for age-related cognitive and cellular change. No published trial has tested meclofenoxate on skin appearance.

sections.h: Use in nootropic and anti-aging communities
paras: Forum discussion of centrophenoxine has been concentrated on bodybuilding and general-health boards such as T Nation, where it appears in long-running 'Brain Function Boosters' threads from 2007 to 2010 as an older European option next to piracetam and choline sources.[18][19][20] Posters describe it in terms of lipofuscin clearance and 'anti-aging', and some describe it as widely used in Europe.[20][22] Reviews of the supplement market list centrophenoxine among unapproved or unauthorised ingredients found in products sold as cognitive enhancers, a finding that regulators and toxicologists have discussed since 2022.[13][15]

Grokipedia's AI-generated entry credits French pharmacologists Jean Thuillier, Germaine Thuillier and Paul Rumpf of the CNRS in Paris with synthesising the compound in 1959, with French patenting in 1960 and European sale as Lucidril from around 1970; these details come from a single non-peer-reviewed source.[17]

Meclofenoxate entered clinical use in Europe and Japan as Lucidril, and the controlled human studies in the published literature date from the late 1960s to 1990.[8][10] A 1968 Japanese double-blind trial examined it for dizziness after head injury, and the compound has been prescribed in Japan for that indication since.[8][17]

The 26.5 percent mouse lifespan finding, reported for meclofenoxate and DMAE, helped establish its image as an anti-aging compound.[1] Grokipedia dates a seminal mouse study to 1974, describing reduced neuronal lipofuscin and about a quarter-plus rise in maximum lifespan, and lists later human studies in the 1970s through 2000s that it describes as mostly small, short or methodologically limited.[17]

On the T Nation 'Brain Function Boosters' threads (2007-2010), posters asked about and recommended centrophenoxine alongside piracetam-type nootropics, and one 2009 post described it as an anti-aging drug widely used in Europe to increase brain energy.[18][19][20] Brazil's 2023 control listing and the supplement-regulation reviews are the main regulatory events.[1][15]

lore.intro: On T Nation nootropic threads, centrophenoxine is mentioned as an older European anti-aging nootropic, usually for its claimed lipofuscin-clearing effect.[18][21]

claims.claim: It clears lipofuscin, the age pigment that builds up in the brain
claims.believers: Posters describe it as removing age-related pigment and reasoning that this restores brain function; one forum user says it clears accumulated 'plaque' from drug use, trauma and aging.[21][22]
claims.experts: A 1978 study reported that meclofenoxate reduces neuronal lipofuscin and noted earlier reports of mental improvement, while cautioning that these findings come from small older studies; animal studies describe the reduction.[7][17]

claims.claim: It improves memory and general brain function
claims.believers: Forum users group it with piracetam, choline sources and other nootropics as a way to keep the brain 'powered up' for learning and training.[18][19]
claims.experts: A 1977 double-blind study in elderly volunteers reported improved consolidation of new information on some memory tests.[6]

claims.claim: It slows aging and extends lifespan
claims.believers: Posters describe it as an 'anti-aging' compound that removes an age-correlated pigment.[22]
claims.experts: The 26.5 percent lifespan increase was reported in mice; no human lifespan study has been published.[1]

claims.claim: It is a safe, well-tolerated cholinergic
claims.believers: Users describe it as widely used in Europe and generally well tolerated.[20]
claims.experts: Reported adverse effects are rare and include insomnia, dizziness, restlessness and headache; regulators in the US have not approved it and reviews list it among unauthorized supplement ingredients.[1][15]

claims.claim: Centrophenoxine shares the skin-firming appeal of DMAE
claims.believers: Because DMAE is the compound it releases and DMAE appears in topical skin-firming products, some anti-aging discussion treats the two as related.
claims.experts: DMAE is used in some skin products, but no published study has tested meclofenoxate on skin; Wikipedia reports no human efficacy data for oral DMAE.[23][1]

angle.text: Meclofenoxate is taken by some people as a general anti-aging nootropic. The proposed route is cellular rather than topical, and its use for visible skin aging has not been studied.
